rationale: Phylogenetic multilevel meta-analysis of male status -> reproductive success across 46 studies in 33 non-industrial societies (Zr=0.19, 95% CI 0.09-0.31). Strengths: cross-cultural aggregation, and restriction to non-industrial societies deliberately limits the contraception confound, which is exactly the moderator this chapter needs. Residual risk is confounding within the pooled observational estimates (status is not assigned) and the heterogeneity of status measures pooled. Cross-population aggregation carries the many-differences risk when read as a contraception contrast.

Zero-order Pearson correlations of personal income with children ever born in a large US administrative sample (men r=+0.070, women r=-0.057). Selection and measurement risk are low given the representative admin frame and self-reported completed fertility, but identification is serious: the estimate is an unadjusted cross-sectional correlation with income endogenous to education, cohort, and preferences. Administrative-scale N drives the standard error to near zero, so precision must not be read as identification.

Zero-order correlations of personal income with number of offspring in NLSY79 (men r=+0.08, women r=-0.15). Representative cohort sample keeps selection low, but the pooled correlation is unadjusted and income is endogenous. Exposure classification is moderate because status is operationalized several ways (income, education, g) with the reported correlation tied to income. Identification serious for the same reason as Hopcroft 2018.

study_label: Fieder et al. 2005 (Ethology; U. Vienna employees)
rationale: Spearman correlations of gross salary with offspring count by age class in University of Vienna employees (male +0.07 to +0.22, female -0.10 to -0.27; representative value male +0.16 n=2693, female -0.18 n=2073). Selection is serious: a single-employer, highly educated workforce is not a general population, which bounds transportability. Reported-result selection is moderate because effects are stratified across six age classes without a single pre-registered summary. Confounding and identification serious as an observational correlation.

Partial correlation of men's income with children ever born, controlling age and current marital status, in the US GSS (r=-0.0195, n=12,084). Selection and measurement low given the representative GSS frame. Confounding is moderate rather than serious because two key covariates are adjusted, but identification remains serious: only two covariates are held fixed, income is still endogenous, and the near-zero partial correlation is descriptive, not causal.
